references.text: The Sabbath commandment in the Ten Commandments forbids work on the Sabbath. The Jews in John 5:10 accuse the healed man of breaking this commandment by carrying his bed on the Sabbath. Exodus 20:10 is the basis for their accusation.

The holiness of the Sabbath is further emphasized in Exodus 31:13-17, where profaning the Sabbath is described as a very serious matter. This provides background for the strong reaction from the Jews in John 5:10.

In Jeremiah 17:21-22, the Lord explicitly warns against carrying burdens on the Sabbath day. The Jews in John 5:10 implicitly refer to this tradition when they say it is not permitted to carry a bed on the Sabbath.

Nehemiah rebukes the people for carrying burdens on the Sabbath in Nehemiah 13:15-19. This shows the Old Testament background for the prohibition against carrying things on the Sabbath, which is the basis for the accusation in John 5:10.

In John 7:23, Jesus himself points out that actions are performed on the Sabbath (circumcision), and argues that healing on the Sabbath should also be allowed. This is a direct follow-up to the conflict that began in John 5:10.

In John 9:14-16, a similar conflict arises where Jesus heals on the Sabbath, and the Pharisees accuse him of breaking the Sabbath. The parallel to John 5:10 is clear — Sabbath healings repeatedly create conflicts with the Jewish leaders.
In Luke 13:14, the synagogue ruler reacts with anger because Jesus healed on the Sabbath. This parallel shows the same pattern as in John 5:10, where religious leaders oppose healing on the Sabbath.

In Mark 2:23-24, the Pharisees accuse the disciples of doing something unlawful on the Sabbath (picking grain). This is a parallel to John 5:10, where the Jews accuse the healed man of an action they consider unlawful on the Sabbath.

In John 5:16-18, the conflict that began in John 5:10 escalates — the Jews persecute Jesus because he did this on the Sabbath, and Jesus responds by calling God his Father, which provokes them further.
